translations.title: To a Nightingale
translations.text:
April, flying, living spring,
so alive that, deceived by your colors,
time gave you flowers as punishment,
for winter is cruel to its scant life.

You did not die; you flew to a higher sphere,
for Phyllis today enlivens you with sorrows;
it is right that he who sang of love should die—
I know one who is silent, though dying of love.

You sought your death, to see yourself
pitied by one who lives untouched
by sorrow for a living lover.

Oh, wretched in life and in death!
Alive, you did not cause her a lover's pain;
dead, her care does you no good.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: I Live So Free of Love
translations.text:
I live so free of love, and have lived so,
that willingly I taste its pain,
giving exercise to all the resistance
that rests within my hardened breast.

I gaze upon the flame from a safe distance,
by freedom's habit, not by prudence;
for beauty, whose appearance is its soul,
needs only the risk to one sense.

Let him flee the sea who, safe on shore,
saw the clear dangers of the drowned;
let him not trust the sea for a divine light.

For heaven reserves its mercy
for one who groans, bound to his ruin,
not for him who builds his own.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Hell Grew Here, Violent Nile
translations.text:
Hell grew here, violent Nile of flames,
so blind in its enmity
that it left no witness to its rage
nor let one sigh escape its devastation.

Such a wonder did not seem heaven-sent
(even disguised as a friend in vengeance),
for heaven, between omen and punishment,
always left room for repentance.

Vesuvius burned; Jupiter's harshness
did not honor its faithless fainting,
nor did his trident drown it in watery bolts.

He whose soul is violence
needs no lightning bolt to die,
for an accident is born already struck.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: I, Who Once with Cheerful Countenance
translations.text:
I, who once with cheerful countenance
raised a sacred altar to fleeing Love,
now yield my freedom, still defended,
to your dominion, though I could refuse it.

For if, fearing love, I remain captive
in the greatest pain, the pain I fear,
he loses neither freedom nor risks life
who asks not to die of the blow through fear.

And though my courage lacks no strength,
against the vengeance of your quiver, Love,
from today I follow your victorious arms.

Loving, I shall escape—not death,
for fear of dying also caused it—
the shame of dying without an enemy.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Gerardo, Who Grieves over His Repeated Error
translations.text:
Gerardo, who grieves over his repeated error,
though soon he grieve amid a thousand horrors,
deserves the sun of eternal splendors,
in recompense for night's oblivion.

But whoever does not break the laws of sense
asks heaven's favor in vain;
the mighty aid that overcomes our errors
is often late when one must be lost.

What matters if I say that I am sailing
toward the port that disillusion leads to,
if my soul now hides its idols?

But, my lord, if error is blind,
it knew how to lose its sight—and that was harm,
for when it weeps, it opens its eyes wider.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Loving Nightingale, Who Give to the Wind
translations.text:
Loving nightingale, who give to the wind
the laments where my hope makes its home;
though wind is the image of change,
only there does my sorrow dwell at rest.

In you the arm that reaches every life
disturbed the peace of your element;
it wounded me too, but with greater force,
when envy strikes its most violent blow.

One blow alone dealt death to us both
(so do not claim the matter for yourself):
my eyes, while bullets struck you.

Oh, how much better fortune was yours!
Love wounds you and leaves you feathered,
so you may chase your offender on wings.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Reef In the Daring Winged Sail
translations.text:
Reef in the daring, winged sail,
Palinurus, who saw the furious sea;
it would be an insult (the powerful do that)
just to see you armed for your defense.

Let the oar fall silent, even the vow be still;
working is idle when the hour is right.
Effort is wasted on one destined for happiness,
if that is to come through being forgotten.

Surrender is a wise sacrifice
where resistance cannot prevail;
frustrated fury lasts and grows.

For heaven did not make violence
so absolute—and still less when wind arms it—
that in the end it cannot be overcome by obedience.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Wise Marquis, with Whom Apollo Shares
translations.text:
Wise Marquis, with whom Apollo shares
the laurel that crowns so many,
while Mars reserves another glorious half-circle
for his foreseen triumphs;

tell me: why does Love always allot
pain, tears, and jealous disdain
to his own? If it is love, how can it be hateful?
If divinity offends through art, is that art?

I confess that pleasure sometimes prefers
pain, but when has pleasure ever managed
to reduce its moments to a single delight?

Why is Love blind, though he aims and wounds,
while lovers who follow him, knowing he is unjust,
are never called blind?
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Hearing at Sea
translations.text:
Now the sun is failing; sea and sky, at rest,
joined, conceal the distant shore;
a bird of metal breaks the air,
flying in voice as far as flight is denied.

Unhappy child of African soil,
stolen from the harshness of the chain,
today you make music betray your sorrow
(if sorrow can exist where comfort is found).

Let your voice sound, though less than mine, captive,
for your trumpet follows the oar,
and you alternate groaning with song.

While I, condemned to Venus' sea,
pass from one extreme of love to another,
and, because it would ease me, even tears are denied.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Two Shipwrecks Meet in Equal Opposition
translations.text:
Two shipwrecks meet in equal opposition
for her whose beauty surpassed Narcissus,
when she wished to imitate him in the waters,
giving her suns a liquid setting.

Licio sees her less present in the sea
than in himself, where a more certain gulf burns.
He grieves he cannot save her—oh, blind warning!—
where he sees her, not where he feels her.

But, Licio, your affection is well governed:
where she might die, that you cannot aid her
is what your love feels, not the blindness.

For in your breast, though burning, she will be eternal;
in water she would live in doubt,
for water has no phoenix, while fire has one.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Epilogue
translations.text:
And at last silence reigns.

For always, even unwillingly,
we keep a secret.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Mortal Counsel
translations.text:
Raise your building. Plant a tree.

Fight if you are young. And make love—ah, always!

But do not forget at last to build with your triumphs

what you need most: a tomb, a refuge.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Night Comes Naked
translations.text:
The night comes naked:

moon breasts,
purple gloves.

With arms raised
I am already waiting for her.
How close to my ear
her lips fall silent!

Love, love!
Death
is kissing me.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Near and Far
translations.text:
Beyond sin,
indescribable, I adore you,
and when I search for words
I find only kisses.

On your chest, your nape,
I love you.
In the secret chalice,
I love you

where your belly curves,
your back flees,
your body is fragrant—
I love you.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Beyond Sin...
translations.text:
Beyond sin,
indescribable, I adore you,
and when I search for words
I find only kisses.

On your chest, your nape,
I love you.
In the secret chalice,
I love you.

where your belly curves,
your back flees,
your body is fragrant—
I love you.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: In the Clear Morning, the Gods’ Laughter...
translations.text:
In the clear morning, the gods' laughter
thunders like a storm.
The underground bull lifts its head,
and trees tremble, rich with leaves.

Transparent tempest. Blue! And suddenly
a faint feminine smile, lost,
silences the great powers,
and seems to say something.
But it says nothing.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Life, Nothing More
translations.text:
Life that murmurs. Life wide open.
Life smiling, always restless.
Life that flees, turning its head,
temptress, or perhaps just a mischievous child.
Life, nothing more. Blind life
that wants to be lived without great consequences,
without gestures, without historic hysterias,
without transcendent pain or triumphant joy,
light, only light, simply beautiful,
or what on earth we usually call so.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Weariness, the Immense...
translations.text:
The weariness, the immense
weariness of repeated days.
(All joy presupposes
some heroism.)
Admirable enemy,
I am born of you, suffering.
(To burn: thus I deceive myself
with an illuminated soul.)
And I live from the death
you give me smiling,
and die in the sweetness
of your vague silence.
Beloved, my beloved,
high flame in time,
you create melodies
with pauses and secrets.
And suddenly tedium stretches
into sweet forms,
and days take their names
from a feeling.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: A Man’s Love
translations.text:
My strict will, my dry point
that tames within her
oceanic passions and ancient murmurs. The cautery I apply
to that shapeless, throbbing wound of love.
If I wound, I kill, I engender.
(Her lifeless smile moves and excites me.)
If I caress her, I measure,
I restrain her ambiguities and all
the supreme softnesses that invite us to nothingness.

Until at last, in blood,
in her alone herself,
in my going through my own feelings,
I possess her, kill, die.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: In the Shadowy Chamber...
translations.text:
In the shadowy chamber,
among cold basalts,
the monumental, luminous belly
of a marble statue.
The rain lulled the secrets
and plucked taut strings
on silence's harp,
while an angel, wrapped
in a dazzling halo of mystery,
caressed with indifferent gesture
the goddesses' breasts.
At Venus' feet
the doves fell strangled.
Naked, cold love
slept upon the moonlit edges
of ten shining knives.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Farewell
translations.text:
Perhaps, when I die,
they will say: He was a poet.
And the world, always beautiful, will shine unaware.

Perhaps you will not remember
who I was, but in you will sound
the anonymous verses I once set in the bud.

Perhaps nothing will remain
of me, not a word,
not one of these words I dream today into tomorrow.

But seen or unseen,
but spoken or unspoken,
I shall be in your shadow, O beautifully living ones!

I shall go on going,
I shall go on dying,
I shall be, I know not how, part of the great concert.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: That Life Which Is Not Mine and Surrounds Me...
translations.text:
That life which is not mine and surrounds me,
the mystery of death, what we call death,
and the mystery of life, always open,
what we call life
in the tree, in clouds and water,
in wind and in the world that is itself without humankind,
in the immense transparency that is not spoken, but shown
in what I sought so long and now find as I return:
childhood, perhaps, childhood, our certain end,
our tale, our song, our magical awareness:
the whole of the infinite and open life.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Final Dedication
translations.text:
But you exist there. Beside me. So close!
You bite an apple. And the apple exists.
You frown. You laugh. You are existing.
And you open your eyes so wide you kill my fear,
and give me the bitten apple that I bite.
So real is what I live, so false what I think
that—enough!—I kiss you!
To hell with verses,
and Don One, Saint X, and N plus Zero!
I am still alive, thanks to your love, my love,
and though all this is absurd, everything exists because you exist;
if you shine, there is no void, no reason for suicide,
no logical consequence. Because I live in you, I live myself,
and once again, thanks to you, I feel like a child.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Life Is So Simple
translations.text:
Life is so simple it explains itself,
it is enough unto itself.
Look! Everything is made. Everything is given.
We need only accept
or perhaps—we are human—praise
and sing
to what shapes us without allowing thought.
Everything is here. Don't you see?
There is no reason, no beyond.
We are happy! We live the explosive moments
of joy or pain, rage or love,
and if not,
then we are distracted, bored.
There is nothing to await. Nothing to fear.
Death, too,
will come when it is faithfully needed,
and we shall receive it with true eagerness.
Since birth
we have been preparing to be consumed.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Two of Them Went Dressed with Defiance...
translations.text:
The two of them went dressed with defiance
(miniskirt, long hair),
hand in hand,
so young they almost frightened you,
so absorbed in a zero
that, though unseen, joined them as absolutes,
something fiercely pure.
They went anywhere, hand in hand.
They loved without sadness,
or joy, or anything.
Sometimes they looked at each other, but did not see.
Then they sat on some bench.
But they did not see.
She was very pretty; she seemed dazed;
he was fierce and scrawny.
They did not speak. They had nothing more to say.
They no longer desired each other.
But they stayed together, hand in hand,
facing something terrifying.

While the transistor radio kept playing.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Biography
translations.text:
Don't hold the spoon in your left hand.
Don't put your elbows on the table.
Fold your napkin neatly.
That's how to begin.

Extract the square root of three thousand three hundred thirteen.
Where is Tanganyika? In what year was Cervantes born?
I'll give you a zero for conduct if you speak to your classmate.
That's how to go on.

Do you think it proper for an engineer to write verse?
Culture is an ornament; business is business.
If you keep seeing that girl, we'll close our doors to you.
That's how to live.

Don't be so crazy. Be polite. Be proper.
Don't drink. Don't smoke. Don't cough. Don't breathe.
Ah yes, don't breathe! Say no to every no.
And rest: die.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: And Night Rises Like Music in the Making...
translations.text:
And night rises like music still in the making,
and stars shine, trembling at their extinction,
and the cold, the clear cold,
the world's great cold,
the scant reality of all I see and touch,
the little love I find,
move me to seek you,
woman, in a certain forest of warm heartbeats.
Only you, my sweet,
sweet with the scents of thick, strong sap,
speechless, so near, throbbing with me,
only you are real in a counterfeit world;
I touch you, and believe you,
and you are the warm, soft womb of realities,
lover, shelter, mother,
or earth's weight, which I caress only in you,
or a presence that lasts when I close my eyes,
outside me, so beautiful.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: At Night
translations.text:
And night rises like music still in the making,
and stars shine, trembling at their extinction,
and the cold, the clear cold,
the world's great cold,
the scant reality of all I see and touch,
the little love I find,
move me to seek you,
woman, in a certain forest of warm heartbeats.

Only you, my sweet,
sweet with the scents of thick, strong sap,
speechless, so near, throbbing with me,
only you are real in a counterfeit world;
I touch you, and believe you,
and you are the warm, soft womb of realities,
lover, shelter, mother,
or earth's weight, which I caress only in you,
or a presence that lasts when I close my eyes,
outside me, so beautiful.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Tell Me How You Live (How You Are Dying)
translations.text:
Tell me how you live;
tell me simply how your days pass,
your slow hatreds, your joyful gunpowder,
and the confused waves that carry you lost
in the shifting foam of an unforeseen whiteness.

Tell me how you live.
Come to me, face to face;
tell me your lies (mine are worse),
your resentments (I suffer them too),
and that foolish pride (I can understand you).

Tell me how you die.
Nothing of yours is secret:
the nausea of the void (or pleasure, it is the same);
the unforeseen madness of some living instant;
the hope that stubbornly deepens the void.

Tell me how you die,
how you renounce—as a sage—,
how—as a frivolous soul—you shine, pure fugitive,
how you end in nothing
and plainly teach me to remain calm.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Transparent Mirrors
translations.text:
One says what one says, but not what one thinks.
Mirrors do not reflect: they make transparent.
Everything looks fascinating face-on, yet does not exist.
Everything returns from behind and is real, invisible.
In what I see, I do not see; in what I do not see, I believe;
in every image a manyfold presence points,
the heart's throbbing flicker: confusion;
and so I feel uncertain, like a poor lost man,
like you—who are you?—like me—who am I?

The mirrors that spit me outward and inward
offer transparencies of distance and silence;
they must be, I want them to be, examples for my work,
with much light outside, more secrecy within.
I play the game, yes, with a cheat, as verses are double.

Thus we tell the things that happen to us each day,
and well told, they seem fascinating and soulless.
If one thinks, nothing is what the mirror shows.
The great light is an abyss and a foolish mystery.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: At the Bottom of the Night the Silver Waters Tremble
translations.text:
At the bottom of the night the silver waters tremble.
The moon is a dead cry in delirious eyes.
With a halo of silence
the glass-headed sleepwalkers pass,
they pass like someone sighing,
they pass among transparent green ice.
It is the hour of crimson roses and steel daggers
upon bodies made deathly white by cold.
At the bottom of the night the tree of silence trembles;
men scream so loudly that only the moon can be heard.
It is the hour when children faint upon pianos,
the hour of statues at the transparent bottom of the waters,
the hour when at last everything seems possible.
At the bottom of the night the tree of silence trembles.
Tell me what you saw, you who stood with your heads turned away.
The stillness of this hour is a silence that listens;
silence is the stealth of approaching death.
Tell me what you saw.
At the bottom of the night
bodies shiver, chilled through.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Esparto Grass, Salt, Granite...
translations.text:
Esparto grass, salt, granite,
what is strictly dry, ardently white,
the indivisible fury in absolute light
of a sun at its zenith and empty space.

Abrasive stones and dazzled lime.
Quartz and its burst of tiny stars
buried in the insides of what cannot be explained.
And the splendor of a world without meaning.

Here, in the insides: rock, light, fury, dryness,
violent details, sometimes luminous;
and the fabric of air, the quivering linen
between the light fingers of a suggestive breeze.

I say it, and saying it, recall accounts, tales
Pliny recorded with substantial names:
the acorn, clay, holm oak, and pig iron,
wine and vitriol, slate and wax,

rubble, electrum, burning quicksilver,
sliding oil, black or white lead,
carbasus, figs, sea squill,
salt in blocks, mineral water, and rabbit.

The light of metals: their sacred encounters,
and at night, buried, their thousand burning waters,
and gold's fury, a red, flaming lion,
and ardent air's blue, hard, arrested splendor.

Furies! Dominions! Devouring gods!
Blind velocities! And suddenly, before the sun,
a hallucinated cry that spins around itself,
that might, that could be who knows what.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Spain on the March
translations.text:
We are who we are.
Enough of history and stories!
Let the dead be! Let them bury their dead as God commands.

We do not live from the past,
nor wind up memory.
We are murky and fresh, a water rushing over its source.

We are the being that grows.
We are a straight river.
We are the fearful beat of an unresolved heart.

We are barbarous, simple.
We are, unto death, Iberian,
who have never yet managed to appear pure, whole, and true.

We feed on all that was,
growing as we transform,
and so we are who we are, blow by blow and dead by dead.

To the streets! The hour has come
to walk out in our own skin
and show that, since we live, we announce something new.

I do not deny my origins,
but I say that we shall be
much more than what is known, the forces of a beginning.

Spaniards with a future,
and Spaniards who, because they are so,
though they embody the past, cannot call it good.

I remember our errors
with bitter spite and a fair wind.
Wrath and light, father Spain, I wake you from your sleep.

I say again who you are.
I think of you again, suspended.
I fight again as it matters, and begin where I begin.

I will not justify you
as a pettifogging lawyer would;
I would be a poet and write your first verse.

My Spain, struggle
that torments my inmost self,
to save myself and save you, I spell you out with love.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Low Voices
translations.text:
It has been here for some hours now.
Parts of her body, not the
		most intimate,
but parts of her body have spread
and
		been scattered in the four or twenty corners
of this room: And now
		I live
inside the thing I love.
A movement I make,
		that stretches me
out of my den, touches a stocking,
a shoe, a
	skirt or a sweater:
the bounds of a land that is mine.

		Version by José Agustín Goytisolo
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Midmorning
translations.text:
Womb


It has been here for some hours now.
Parts of her body, not the
		most intimate,
but parts of her body have spread
and
		been scattered in the four or twenty corners
of this room: And now
		I live
inside the thing I love.
A movement I make,
		that stretches me
out of my den, touches a stocking,
a shoe, a
	skirt or a sweater:
the bounds of a land that is mine.

		Version by José Agustín Goytisolo
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: 2nd. This Long Weariness...
translations.text:
Riches
I have my
		faithful joy
and my lost joy:
one like a rose,
the other like a thorn.
What they stole from me,
I was not dispossessed of:

		I have my faithful joy
and my lost joy,
and I am rich in purple

		and melancholy.
Ah, how loving is the rose
and how beloved the thorn!

		Like the double outline

of twin fruits,
I have my faithful joy
and my
		lost one....
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Love That Is Silent
translations.text:
If I hated you, my hatred would be given
to you in words, firm and sure;
but I love you, and my love does not trust
this speech of men, so dark.

You would have it turned to a shriek,
but it comes from so deep it has spent
its burning flood, exhausted,
before the throat, before the breast.

I am like a brimming pond,
and to you I seem an inert fountain.
All because of my troubled silence,
more atrocious than entering death!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Little Feet
translations.text:
Little feet of a child,
blue with cold,
how people see you and do not cover you,
my God!

Little wounded feet
by every pebble,
violated by snow
and mud!

Blind man does not know
that wherever you pass,
a flower of living light
you leave;

that where you set
your bleeding little foot,
the nard grows more
fragrant.

Since you walk
along straight roads,
be heroic, as you are,
perfect.

Little feet of a child,
two suffering jewels,
how people pass by
without seeing you!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: To My Son’s Face...
translations.text:
On my son's face,
as he sleeps, come down
sands from the dunes,
sugarcane blossom,
and foam that flies
from the waterfall…

And all that falls on him
is only dream;
dream falls on his mouth,
dream on his back,
and they steal his body
along with his soul.

And so they cover him
with such cunning
that in the night I have
no son, nothing,
a mother blind with shadow,
a mother robbed.

Until blessed sun
at last bathes him:
it gives him back to me as a lovely
peeled fruit
and places him whole
upon my lap!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Awakening
translations.text:
We slept; I dreamed the Southern Land,
dreamed the whole Valley,
the pasture, the curly vineyard,
and the glory of the orchards.
What did you dream, my Child,
with such a peaceful face?

Let's go look for chañar trees
until we find them,
and guillaves hanging
at kiosks in hell.
Whoever gathers most invites
two others who gathered none.
I do not prick my hands
on the mist from which they were born.
I am not hungry, nor thirsty, and
without virtue I give or yield.
Why thank me so
for fruit I take and hand away?
